## Abstract

First‐in‐human pig xenotransplant clinical trials may soon begin, which raises ethical concerns about patients’ decision‐making to participate in such trials. We assessed kidney transplant candidates’ attitudes and hypothetical decision‐making about participating in xenotransplant trials through semi‐structured telephone interviews and an online survey. We analyzed qualitative data by thematic analysis and quantitative data by descriptive statistics. Twenty‐eight patients participated in interviews; 142 patients participated in the survey. Most interview and survey respondents were male (68%, 56%), White (54%, 61%), or Black (36%, 22%). Although interview participants appreciated xenotransplantation research's potential to advance science, they expressed concerns about infection transmission and graft function. Few survey respondents were willing to participate in a pig kidney trial to test the safety of pig kidneys (12.6%) or pig kidney function (16.9%). Interview participants would be more likely to participate in a first‐in‐human pig kidney trial if receiving a human kidney was unlikely and their health status declined. Willingness would also depend on how long the pig kidney would function. Most interview participants were receptive to long‐term monitoring, but not to family monitoring. Transplant programs planning xenotransplant trials should anticipate these types of concerns for optimizing human subject protections and conducting a robust informed consent process.

## Introduction

Xenotransplantation, or the transplantation of organs from non‐human animals into human recipients, is a highly promising approach for potentially alleviating the organ shortage. Research over the past 25 years involving transplanting genetically modified pig kidneys into nonhuman primates [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] supports a scientific foundation for launching clinical trials with living human recipients [1, 5, 6]. Studies involving five xenotransplants with gene‐edited kidneys to deceased humans [2, 7, 8, 9, 10] provided mostly promising, albeit with some mixed, evidence of pig kidneys producing urine, creatinine clearance, and graft survival. As of November 2024, three living humans have received a pig kidney under the US Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) expanded access/compassionate use program for patients with serious or immediately life‐threatening diseases/conditions who lack alternative interventions and when clinical trial participation is not possible [10, 11].

Developers of source pigs for xenotransplantation plan to request FDA approval to conduct the first clinical trials with living humans [12, 13]. Enrolling patients in these trials may be challenging due to uncertain risks and benefits to participants [3, 14]. Although surgical risks for xenotransplantation may be comparable to allotransplantation, the possibility of a pig kidney transmitting known and unknown infectious diseases to human recipients requires additional surveillance [15, 16] much like using HIV+ and HCV+ donor organs [17]. Unlike many zoonotic diseases, however, HIV+/HCV+ organ recipients undergo surveillance for a short period and effective treatments exist for HIV/HCV. This elevates the trial's risk profile for individual and public health. Additionally, some patients may object morally to using animal organs in humans regardless of outcomes [18, 19]. Moreover, while some studies report pig xenograft survival rates in non‐human primates of just over 2 years, whether this survival rate will be similar in human recipients is unknown [20, 21]. The first living recipient of a pig kidney returned home 2‐weeks post‐transplant, but died almost 2 months post‐transplant. The second recipient, who also received a heart pump, started dialysis after the pig kidney was removed 47 days post‐transplant due to challenges from the combination heart/kidney transplant, and has since died [22, 23]. It is too soon to know how long future pig kidney recipients will survive and if survival will reach or exceed 2 years, as reported for non‐human primates.

Understanding patient perspectives is essential for addressing potential barriers to participation and ethical concerns in xenotransplant trials, enhancing study feasibility, acceptability, and recruitment. Extensive US and international research and a meta‐analysis have demonstrated generally high rates of acceptance of xenotransplantation as a clinical treatment option if outcomes were comparable to allotransplantation (e.g., 75.3%–76%) [4, 24] and positive attitudes [4, 25], while one large‐scale US survey by Padilla et al. found more moderate levels of acceptance (45%–55%) [26]. Demographic factors associated with lower acceptance include younger age, female gender, and racial minority status [26, 27]. Padilla et al. also found that despite the dearth of xenotransplant outcomes data, 36% of respondents were amenable to experimental xenotransplantation if they needed a transplant [26]. However, little is known about patients’ attitudes specifically toward participating in first‐in‐human xenotransplant clinical trials. Only one focus group study of n = 27 community members in Alabama reported a high level of acceptance of the idea that xenotransplant trials could increase organ availability, and identified concerns, but did not examine willingness to participate in a trial per se [28]. Although most of the 20 patients and 10 caregivers interviewed through The National Kidney Foundation‐sponsored initiative expressed support for xenotransplant clinical trials, nine (30%) reported being “likely” or “very likely” to participate in a xenotransplant trial, but did not provide qualitative reasons for participants’ rationales [29]. Therefore, we aimed to qualitatively and quantitatively assess waitlisted kidney patients’ attitudes in‐depth about participating in a first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trial.

## Materials and Methods

### Study Design

We conducted a convergent, parallel mixed‐methods study involving semi‐structured interviews and online surveys to assess waitlisted kidney patients’ qualitative perceptions and the strength of attitudes about participating in first‐in‐human pig kidney trials [30].

Our multi‐site study was conducted at Northwestern University (NU) in Chicago, IL, USA; Lehigh University (LU) in Bethlehem, PA, USA; and The Hastings Center (HC) in Garrison, NY, USA. Rutgers University in affiliation with the Robert Wood Johnson (RWJ) transplant program in Piscataway, NJ, assisted LU with recruiting participants. Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) at NU (STU00214874) and LU (1806245‐5) approved the study. NU served as the IRB of record. We used the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research for quality reporting of qualitative studies [31], and the Checklist for Reporting of Survey Studies for quality reporting of survey results [32].

### Participants and Recruitment

Eligible participants included English‐speaking, adult (age ≥18 years), “active” (and “inactive” at NU only) waitlisted kidney patients. Patients wait‐listed for multiple organ transplants and/or who were cognitively impaired were excluded. We recruited patients for interviews and surveys at NU and RWJ by obtaining an IRB‐approved partial HIPAA waiver for a list of eligible names and contact information then emailing and/or mailing letters to introduce the study. For interview recruitment, research staff called patients a week later to assess interest and schedule an interview. Survey recruitment emails included a link unique to the individual to the online consent form and survey in REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) [33]; patients were sent up to four reminder emails over 5 weeks and survey settings prevented multiple responses from patients. Research staff did not have prior relationships with study participants. Patients provided verbal (interview) or online (survey) informed consent.

### Data Collection

We conducted semi‐structured interviews by telephone from July 2022 to February 2023, and online surveys from November 2022 to June 2023, using an interview guide and survey instrument, respectively, developed from literature reviews and feedback from the study's Ethics and Policy Advisory Committee. The Committee included 17 stakeholders (e.g., transplant recipients, translational researchers, transplant clinicians, transplant regulators, transplant outcomes experts, a transplant payer, transplant ethicists, and research ethics experts). The multiple Principal Investigators (mPIs) held two 2‐h videoconferences with the Advisory Committee to ensure that the interview guide and survey instrument would comprehensively and accurately address current clinical, ethical, and policy considerations about xenotransplantation.

#### Interviews

Open‐ended questions covered patients’ attitudes about xenotransplantation and trial participation (e.g., monitoring and medical research trustworthiness). Closed‐ended questions included a rating scale of interest in participating in a pig kidney trial across different scenarios that varied by time spent on the waitlist and time before receiving a human kidney (File S1). Interviews also included questions on patients’ demographics, health literacy [34], trust in physicians [35], and clinical characteristics.

During the informed consent process and at the beginning of each interview, research staff defined and described xenotransplantation and xenotransplant trials to provide participants a baseline understanding, and stated they had no relationship with the transplant center. Interviews were conducted by female and male research staff trained by one mPI (E.J.G.), a seasoned qualitative researcher. Telephone cognitive interviews were conducted with six patients (December 2021–May 2022) using standard “think aloud” procedures to ensure interview questions were interpreted as intended and improve question wording [36]. Semi‐structured interviews lasted, on average, 58 min (range: 39–93) and were audio‐recorded and transcribed. Participants were compensated with a $30 e‐gift card.

#### Surveys

The self‐administered online survey assessed kidney transplant candidates’ attitudes regarding xenotransplantation and their hypothetical willingness to participate in first‐in‐human pig kidney clinical trials. We drew upon eight closed‐ended questions from the broader survey for the present analysis. Questions assessed attitudes about xenotransplantation, hypothetical willingness to participate in a pig kidney clinical trial in different scenarios: (a) the trial would test the safety of pig kidneys; (b) the trial would test whether the pig kidney worked; (c) the pig kidney would serve as a bridge to a human transplant; (d) the pig kidney would work for only 6 months; and (e) the pig kidney would work for only 1 year. The survey also assessed demographics, health literacy, trust in medical researchers [37], and clinical characteristics (File S2). Xenotransplantation was defined and described for respondents in the online consent form and survey introduction. Respondents were compensated with a $15 e‐gift card.

### Data Analysis

#### Qualitative Analysis

Qualitative data from the semi‐structured interviews were analyzed for themes and patterns emergent from the data [38] using constant comparative [39] and deductive coding methods [40]. Four analytic retreats were held with the larger research team (led by EJG) to iteratively refine code definitions. Codes were revised to account for new observations until saturation was reached [41]. After finalizing the codebook, two research staff at each study site independently coded transcripts using NVivo (QSR International) until establishing inter‐rater reliability (Kappa > 0.80) [38]. Thereafter, research staff re‐coded all transcripts, resolving coding discrepancies through discussion. Research staff reviewed all coded segments for each code and performed inductive thematic “splitting” to reveal patterns and themes across coded segments [38] and to develop code summaries [42].

#### Quantitative Analysis

Descriptive statistics (e.g., means, standard deviations, frequencies) were used to describe participants’ demographic and clinical characteristics using IBM SPSS Statistics (Version 28). To assess potential demographic and clinical predictors of willingness to participate in first‐in‐human pig kidney trials, we estimated bivariate correlations using Chi‐squared tests for categorical variables, and one‐factor analysis of variance for continuous variables. Potential explanatory variables included: age, gender, ethnicity, race, marital status, education, income, religion, diet, health insurance, health literacy, cause of ESKD, time on dialysis, trust in researchers, comfort on dialysis, and number of prior transplants. We dichotomized responses to the willingness questions as “not at all”, “a little”, or “somewhat” willing versus “very” or “entirely” willing. Significant associations (alpha ≤ 0.05) were included in a multivariate logistic model. We also ran logistic regression models with all potential explanatory variables.

## Results

### Participant Characteristics

Overall, 28 kidney patients were interviewed (NU: n = 20, LU: n = 8, 33% participation rate), and 142 completed the survey (NU: n = 116, LU: n = 26, 13.9% response rate). A total of 1019 patients from both sites received an email invitation for the online survey. Thirty‐four individuals declined to be interviewed, and 15 refused to participate in the online survey. Fourteen individuals indicated willingness to participate in the interview but did not provide informed consent because they could not be reached through multiple follow‐up attempts. Eighteen individuals provided consent to participate but did not take part in the interview (n = 9) or did not respond to survey questions (n = 9), and were not included in the analysis. Most interview and survey participants were male (68% and 56%), White (54% and 61%) or Black (36% and 22%), with a mean age of 49 and 52 years. Interview participants had been on the waitlist for an average of 21.5 months (Tables 1A and 1B). Seven individuals participated in both an interview and survey.

### Perceptions of Xenotransplantation (Interviews)

Most interview respondents (n = 23/27) had heard of xenotransplantation from the media or healthcare providers One respondent was not asked the question. Participants described xenotransplantation as “innovative” and “revolutionary” and appreciated its “phenomenal” life‐saving potential given the organ shortage. Some perceived that xenotransplantation was “advancing science” and “hope for some people” but wanted to hear “success stories” before considering pursuing it for themselves. Several had mixed feelings or no opinion primarily due to a lack of information on xenotransplantation. Those with no opinion were still “trying to figure out” how xenotransplantation functioned. All interview respondents expressed concerns about xenotransplantation. Several (30%, n = 8/27) reported concerns about a pig kidney transmitting an infectious disease to the transplant recipient. Nearly half (n = 13/27) questioned whether a pig kidney would “work in a human body.” Even if a pig kidney was functional, some questioned whether it would “last as long as a human kidney” given that the “animal life expectation is less than a human being.” Others expressed concern about a higher risk of rejection than a human kidney and described animals as “built different” than humans. Among the few who knew about a pig heart transplanted into a living recipient, the 2‐month survival “threw a red flag up” regarding xenotransplantation's potential viability. These respondents wanted to understand why the recipient only lived for 2 months and whether a pig kidney would last a similar length of time.

### Attitudes About Xenotransplant Trials (Interviews and Surveys)

A subset of interview respondents (n = 7/27) thought that experiencing kidney failure or rejection within a clinical trial could be worse than remaining on dialysis and waiting for a human kidney because dialysis, human kidneys, and immunosuppressants are “well‐tested,” while xenotransplantation is replete with “unknowns.”

By contrast, most survey respondents expressed support for the idea of xenotransplant trials.

Nearly all “strongly agreed” or “agreed” that participating in xenotransplant clinical trials gives patients “the chance to help advance science” (93.7%) and “the chance to help other patients in the future” (94.4%) (Table 3). ### Trustworthy Research (Interviews)

Interview respondents identified three factors that would make a pig kidney clinical trial trustworthy: success stories, transparency, and institutional reputation. Respondents indicated they would be more likely to trust a pig kidney trial if the research team could provide prior “success stories.” They desired information on how many patients had received pig kidneys, whether the transplants were safe and successful, and on recipient survival and longevity. A few respondents emphasized the importance of transparency and trust when conveying data to potential study participants. Respondents wanted to be “fully informed” about “the good and the bad” so they could make an “intelligent decision.” Some respondents noted that the “reputation” and “credibility” of the institution and research team conducting the trial influenced perceptions of trustworthiness. Respondents desired knowing the “motivations of the organization” and the qualifications of the research team.

### Monitoring (Interviews)

Interview respondents were informed that receiving a pig kidney through a trial could require additional monitoring, beyond that expected with allotransplantation, to ensure that the pig kidney does not transmit infectious diseases. Most respondents (n = 21/28) were receptive to this idea and described the additional monitoring as an expected “part of the process.” Potential monitoring steps were perceived as “a minor inconvenience” compared to patients’ experiences of dialysis monitoring. Others expressed a desire to be monitored to detect potential rejection and to ensure the pig kidney remained healthy.

Most interview respondents (n = 21/28) would accept being monitored for “as long as the research team would feel necessary.” Some proposed ideal timeframes, including 6 months to a year, a few years, and 5 years. Over half (n = 19/28) said they were amenable to lifetime monitoring, while those opposed (n = 9/28) acknowledged that perpetual monitoring sounded “inconvenient” or like “an infraction on your privacy,” expecting monitoring to eventually “lighten up” if the pig kidney was “doing fine.”

A few interview respondents accepted the idea of their family being monitored if they were to get an infectious disease from a pig kidney. However, most (n = 20/28) expressed reservations and described such monitoring as “awkward” or “a concern.” Before accepting a pig kidney, some would want to consult their family about the “possible repercussions” of study participation. One participant stated, “Probably less comfortable because now, this is my fight, not theirs, and now they have to be inconvenienced.” Others described monitoring family as “a big problem,” with a few stressing that they would feel “horrible” about family members losing “privacy” and that monitoring could potentially “jeopardize” their family members’ health and “quality of life.” For them, monitoring family members would pose a barrier to trial participation.

Others were unwilling to accept a pig kidney in the first two scenarios but were willing to “consider it” in the third scenario.

### Trade‐offs

#### Interviews

Both interview and survey responses revealed a similar pattern: while participants generally supported xenotransplantation research, they expressed more hesitancy about personal participation in trials, with willingness increasing in scenarios of greater medical urgency. Three different thematic sentiments emerged about participating in a pig kidney trial if doing so meant being less likely to receive a human kidney transplant in the future. Nearly half of the interview respondents (n = 13/28) responded negatively, preferring to keep their “options open” and not “jeopardize” the “opportunity” to receive a human kidney, given human kidney transplants’ known success rates. A few others were unsure, preferring a human kidney and construing a pig kidney as an “alternative.” By contrast, some respondents expressed a positive sentiment, preferring to “just go for it,” motivated by leaving dialysis and having a functioning kidney, despite the risk of not receiving a human kidney in the future.

## Discussion

Our mixed‐methods study provides novel insights into kidney patients’ attitudes about participating in a first‐in‐human pig kidney trial by highlighting factors that would influence decision‐making about trial participation. We found high levels of support for kidney xenotransplant clinical trials, as corroborated by other research [29].

A key finding was mixed willingness to participate in a xenotransplant trial, similar to other research [29]. Some participants reported willingness to be early adopters, while others required evidence of xenotransplant's efficacy and information about the likelihood of success, benefits, and risks before considering participation. The National Kidney Foundation's study participants desired similar information and additional information (e.g., how pig kidneys were being modified) [29, 43]. In research with pediatric cardiac providers and parents, the concern about the genetic modification of pigs also affected clinicians’ and parents’ support of heart xenotransplantation [4]. The absence of scientific studies to provide such information for the informed consent process may pose a challenge to trial recruitment. As with any first‐in‐human clinical trial, human participants are needed, yet potential participants may desire more information than is available. The challenge with recruitment is that first‐in‐human trials are necessary to generate desired information. Overcoming this catch‐22 is necessary to make incremental scientific progress. The information gained about each xenotransplant trial participant will be valuable for refining the informed consent process for subsequent participants.

Our interview participants reported an increased willingness to participate in a xenotransplant trial if their hypothetical time already spent on dialysis would extend from 1 year to 5 years. Participants’ responses make sense given that patients who have been on dialysis for 5 years have already incurred greater cumulative health damage and the exponential health decline than patients who have been on dialysis for 1 year. Having been on dialysis, our study participants could foresee the greater urgency to obtain a xenotransplant to get off dialysis after several years of dialysis treatment. Moreover, transplant programs explicitly inform patients that their life expectancy is significantly longer with improved quality of life with a transplant than by remaining on dialysis. By contrast, our surveyed participants’ actual time spent on dialysis had no significant relationship with their willingness to participate in a xenotransplant trial. We also found that our surveyed patients with a post‐graduate degree were less willing to participate in xenotransplant trials. Such individuals likely bring a higher level of critical thinking about the potential risks along with a higher level of concern about negative outcomes, which may disincentivize them from participating.

Our hypothetical scenarios illustrated how time on the waitlist and health status shaped patients’ thought processes. As patients become more desperate for treatment and fatigued by dialysis, they may become less risk‐averse, and more risk‐taking and amenable to trial participation, as similarly found by the National Kidney Foundation [43]. Time on the waitlist and health status have been identified as central to kidney transplant patients’ considerations of accepting deceased donor intervention organs and expanded criteria organs [44, 45]. Patients’ poor health may make them particularly vulnerable to the therapeutic misconception, which is manifested when patients fail to “appreciate the distinction between the imperatives of clinical research and of ordinary treatment.” [46] Strategies that may mitigate the therapeutic misconception include ensuring that patients understand they are participating in a first‐in‐human trial primarily to obtain safety information about the pig kidney, that participation in the trial is voluntary, and engaging independent patient advocates.

We envision that patients’ experience of decision‐making and perception of voluntariness would differ for pig kidney xenotransplant trials than for pig heart xenotransplant trials. Recruitment into heart xenotransplant trials may be easier than for kidney xenotransplant trials given the lack of alternative heart treatment options, which heightens the benefit to risk calculus. Therefore, patients’ perceptions of voluntariness may be diminished for heart compared to kidney xenotransplant trials. Heart transplant candidates’ perceptions of decision‐making about participating in pig heart xenotransplant trials require further research.’’

Transplant recipient monitoring for infectious diseases during xenotransplant trials is undergoing deliberation [15]. For other high‐risk transplant innovations (e.g., HIV+, HCV+ transplants) that have required surveillance, the risk profile has centered primarily on the recipient [47, 48]. By contrast, xenotransplant trials must balance the ethical needs of protecting public health with individual autonomy and the right to withdraw from trial participation [49]. Our study revealed novel perspectives of patients’ receptivity to post‐transplant monitoring given prior experience with being monitored. Patients were less receptive if monitoring included close contacts, which was perceived as interference and burdening their loved ones. Although risk of disease transmission is expected to be low depending on the pig used [50, 51], the transplant community does not know what is unknown. Thus, monitoring will be required and may figure into patients’ (un)willingness to participate. These findings are valuable for ensuring that clinical trials are patient‐centered in design.

We found a high level of willingness to participate in a hypothetical xenotransplant trial if the pig kidney served as a bridge to a human kidney and death was otherwise imminent. The National Kidney Foundation found similar support [43]. Other research found less support for the use of pig hearts as a bridge to a human heart among pediatric cardiac providers and parents [4]. It is unclear what contributed to different perspectives given that death would be the alternative in both contexts.

Some participants indicated that they would be more willing to participate in trials if their health was declining, assuming the trial could provide benefit. This finding highlights the need for transplant teams recruiting patients into first‐in‐human xenotransplant trials to determine whether patients exhibit a therapeutic misconception or therapeutic optimism. Although therapeutic misconception refers to patients conflating the goals of research and treatment and therefore inappropriately ascribing clinical benefit to the research, therapeutic optimism refers to hope for the best outcome, which is an ethically reasonable position [52]. Our findings reinforce the need for teams to carefully present xenotransplant trial opportunities to avoid imparting the therapeutic misconception.

First‐in‐human xenotransplant trials may face recruitment challenges due to uncertainty over xenograft graft survival. Consent forms and processes should clearly present the available information about efficacy, graft survival, and disease transmission from studies with non‐human primates, deceased donor xenotransplant recipients, and living human recipients of a pig kidney under the FDA's Expanded Access/Compassionate Use pathway for access to investigational drugs/biologics. However, transplant teams should caution patients about extrapolating outcomes from living recipients of pig kidneys received through the Expanded Access/Compassionate Use pathway to the clinical trial context because of different patient eligibility criteria. The first two patients who received a pig kidney under the Expanded Access/Compassionate Use pathway were near death, and the third was healthier [53]. Teams should avoid conveying a higher level of certainty than available about anticipated potential benefits from a pig kidney xenotransplant.

Strengths of our multi‐site study include geographically diverse locations in US cities with large Black and Hispanic populations. Our mixed‐methods approach provided a broader depth of information than single methods alone. Collaboration with our multidisciplinary Advisory Committee ensured that our instruments included accurate and current questions to generate meaningful data, increasing the validity of our findings.

Our study also has limitations. The inclusion of participants from two centers limits generalizability. We did not include non‐waitlisted patients, who could have provided other perspectives. Although eligibility criteria for participation in pig kidney clinical trials are under debate, we recruited waitlisted patients because emerging sentiment during data collection suggested they would be optimal trial participants [54, 55, 56].

Participants were on the waitlist for an average of 2 years, which may not reflect the views of patients waitlisted longer. Given the early stages of xenotransplant clinical translation, we focused on patients’ hypothetical decision‐making. Future research should assess patients’ actual decision‐making during enrollment into xenotransplant trials. Since three living humans recently received a pig kidney, patients’ perceptions might have changed since we collected our data. However, patients’ perceptions and preferences about clinical trial participation might not have changed because the three living human transplants were not involved in a clinical trial designed to collect systematic outcomes data from participants meeting specific eligibility criteria.

Low participation rates, consistent with web‐based survey response rates [57], may reflect a selection bias of motivated participants raising concerns about generalizability but not about transferability. However, 21% of survey respondents identified as Black, which is within the range of their 30% waitlist eligibility, and 36% of interview respondents identified as Black, which reflects an overrepresentation of their 30% waitlist representation [58]. Additionally, 14.3% interviewed and 14.8% surveyed participants had limited health literacy, similar to kidney transplant candidates (12.4%) reported elsewhere [44]. It is unknown whether our educational materials designed to provide foundational knowledge at the outset of interviews may have primed or allayed patients’ concerns about zoonotic disease transmission or other xenotransplant risks.

## Conclusion

Our findings suggest that some kidney patients would be amenable to participating in first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant trials but would also maintain concerns about participation. Transplant programs planning to conduct trials should take caution in presenting the study purpose to optimize human subject protections.

## Abstract

Transplant programs preparing to initiate first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trials must be especially careful when obtaining participants’ informed consent. Little is known about the kind of information patients want for making an informed decision about trial participation.

We conducted semi‐structured telephone interviews with waitlisted kidney transplant patients about information needs regarding participating in a first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant trial, which guided development of a prototype consent form. Subsequent usability testing interviews sought patient feedback on the consent form. We analyzed qualitative data by thematic analysis and quantitative data by descriptive statistics.

Twenty‐eight patients participated in semi‐structured interviews; 16 patients participated in usability testing interviews. Most interview participants were male (68%, 56%), White (54%, 56%), or Black (36%, 31%), respectively. Interview participants identified five types of information needs: (1) the potential for infection contraction and transmission; (2) risks, benefits, and impact of xenotransplant trials; (3) xenotransplant clinical trial and recipient experience; (4) clinical trial logistics; and (5) the pig and its kidney. Usability testing participants suggested adding details to the prototype. Participants’ preparedness to make a decision about participating in a xenotransplant trial increased after reviewing the prototype (12.5% vs. 31.3%, n.s.).

We identified multiple unique types of information patients desired to make informed decisions about pig kidney xenotransplant trial participation. Transplant programs initiating xenotransplant trials should be prepared to address patients’ information needs to optimize informed decision‐making for trial participation. ## Introduction

Transplanting animal organs into humans—known as xenotransplantation—holds great promise for addressing the limited organ supply and saving lives. Many xenotransplant experts anticipate that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) will permit the conduct of first‐in‐human xenotransplant clinical trials involving gene‐edited pig kidneys to test the safety of these organs in human recipients [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Several transplant surgeons intend to request FDA approval to conduct such trials, indicating that trials may soon commence [6, 7, 8]. Public opinion surveys show high levels of support for xenotransplantation [9, 10], and that some would participate in trials [9, 11], indicating, in part, trial feasibility.

Prior to launching such trials, tailoring the ethical approach to informed consent in the xenotransplant trial context is urgently needed. The FDA's regulations governing research with humans require that specific information be provided to individuals recruited for clinical trials to make an informed decision about participation. However, the regulation has not established protections for first‐in‐human clinical trials in general, for which the ethical stakes of informed consent are higher. Xenotransplant trials raise additional ethical considerations that have not yet been addressed.

The informed consent process for participating in a first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trial will likely be ethically challenging because limited information is available about the safety, efficacy, and potential benefits of transplanting a pig kidney into humans [12, 13], which may make informing patients about the innovation difficult [14]. Moreover, xenotransplant recipients may encounter unknown risks. For example, it is unknown whether the organ might transmit a porcine infectious disease to recipients and their close contacts [15]. The unknown potential to transmit known and unknown diseases from the pig organ to human recipient [16, 17] elevates the risk profile of first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant trials.

The five xenotransplants (2 heart, 3 kidney) performed under the FDA's Expanded Access program [14, 18, 19, 20] provide some information about how xenotransplants functioned in those recipients (e.g., the fact that grafts survived 2 months). However, the different eligibility criteria, different gene‐edited pigs used, and patients’ grave conditions mean that their outcomes are unlikely to be commensurate with clinical trial outcomes. Accordingly, the information disclosed to prospective trial participants about such xenotransplants must be qualified.

Magnifying these challenges is that few, if any, treatment alternatives for patients with end‐stage kidney disease exist, which can render patients vulnerable and undermine voluntary decision‐making [12, 13]. Such vulnerability commonly occurs among patients undergoing innovative surgical procedures for which alternative standard treatments are either ineffective or nonexistent [21]. In regard to first‐in‐human xenotransplant trials, waitlisted candidates may have exhausted all life‐saving options, as in the Expanded Access xenotransplants.

The ethical challenges to informed consent comprise a component of translational research that requires resolution. Current federal regulations (i.e., the National Organ Transplant Act of 1984) lack guidance on informed consent for xenotransplant clinical trials [22]. Organ Procurement and Transplant Network policies only pertain to human organs. Thus, policies on information disclosure may not translate to the xenotransplant context.

Few scholars have made headway in addressing this problem. Padilla and colleagues reviewed The US Department of Health and Human Services nine minimum elements that consent forms must include to protect human subjects, highlighting how these elements should be conveyed in the consent process and in the informed consent form for xenotransplantation [23]. Drawing upon this work, Cooper prepared an informed consent form template tailored to the xenotransplant trial context [24]. However, while Cooper's consent form may reflect what is important for transplant clinicians to disclose, it may not address patients’ information needs. Little is known about what information patients need to decide whether to participate in a xenotransplant clinical trial. The National Academies of Sciences called for greater public engagement with emerging innovative areas of biotechnology and biomedical research [25]. This paper presents kidney transplant candidates’ information needs for making informed decisions about participating in pig kidney first‐in‐human xenotransplant clinical trials.

## Materials and Methods

### Study Design

We conducted a sequential, exploratory mixed‐methods study involving semi‐structured interviews to assess waitlisted kidney patients’ information needs, followed by usability testing interviews to assess perceptions of an informed consent prototype for participating in first‐in‐human pig kidney trials [26].

We conducted a multi‐site study at Northwestern University (NU) in Chicago, IL; Lehigh University (LU) in Bethlehem, PA; and The Hastings Center (HC) in Garrison, NY. Rutgers University (RU) in affiliation with the Robert Wood Johnson (RWJ) transplant program in Piscataway, NJ, aided LU in participant recruitment. Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) at NU (STU00214874) and LU (1806245‐5) approved the study. NU served as the single IRB. The Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research guided quality reporting of qualitative research [27].

### Participants and Recruitment

Eligible individuals were: English‐speaking, adult (age ≥18 years), and waitlisted kidney patients. Patients who were cognitively impaired and/or waitlisted for multiple organ transplants were excluded. NU and RWJ patients were recruited by email and/or mailed letter followed by a call a week later to gauge interest and schedule interviews. The research staff had no prior relationships with study participants. Patients provided verbal informed consent.

### Data Collection

We conducted telephone semi‐structured interviews from July 2022 to February 2023, and usability testing interviews from March 2024 to May 2024, using standardized interview guides guided by extant literature and feedback from the study's Ethics and Policy Advisory Committee. The Committee comprised 17 stakeholders (e.g., transplant recipients, translational researchers, transplant clinicians, transplant regulators, transplant outcomes experts, a transplant payer, transplant ethicists, and research ethics experts). The multiple Principal Investigators (mPIs) held two 2‐hour videoconferences with the Advisory Committee to ensure that the interview guide, usability testing instrument, and informed consent form prototype would expansively and precisely address contemporary clinical, ethical, and policy considerations about xenotransplantation. During the informed consent process and upon initiating each interview, research staff explained the concept of xenotransplantation and xenotransplant trials, and they had no relationship with the transplant center.

#### Semi‐Structured Interviews

Interviews included open‐ended questions about patients’ information needs for considering whether to participate in a pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trial, which comprised a subset of the study data (Supporting Information 1). Interviews also assessed demographics, health literacy [28], and clinical characteristics. One mPI (E.J.G.), an experienced qualitative researcher, trained male and female research staff who conducted interviews. Interviews were audio‐recorded, transcribed, and lasted 58 minutes, on average. Participants received a $30 e‐gift card as compensation.

#### Informed Consent Prototype Development

The informed consent prototype was initially developed through an iterative process whereby four staff (M.M., J.G.S., D.M., and K.T.) independently reviewed information from 19 questions in the semi‐structured interview transcripts pertaining to patients’ information needs for informed consent for trial participation. Using a NU IRB biomedical consent form with template language to fill in as a guide, each staff member developed a draft prototype by transforming the information needs into distinct statements regarding trial purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives, implications for reproduction, and other sections of the consent form, as well as adapting the consent form template language to the xenotransplant study context. One Principal Investigator (E.J.G.) provided initial feedback in simplifying the statement phrasing and organization, guiding the four staff members in revising their drafts and completing transcript reviews. The resulting prototypes were consolidated into one prototype “Master” draft. The mPIs and staff refined this draft for clarification and face validity. Advisory Committee members provided feedback on two sequential versions of the Master prototype. Based on both sets of Advisory Committee feedback, the mPIs revised the Master prototype and submitted it to the NU IRB for approval. After completing usability testing interviews, the staff and mPIs reviewed participants’ suggested changes and further refined the prototype for clarity and provided additional information usability testing participants requested. Supporting Information 2 provides the Prototype Informed Consent Form. The prototype retains some template instructions in red font that trial investigators will need to address.

#### Usability Testing Interviews

We conducted usability testing interviews using cognitive interviewing techniques [29] to elicit patients’ perceptions of the consent form prototype in terms of content comprehensiveness, clarity, and order, and suggestions for improvement. Participants were asked before and after reviewing the prototype: “How prepared do you feel to make a decision about participating in a pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trial?” using a 5‐point Likert scale anchored by “not at all likely” and “entirely likely.” Interviews lasted, on average, 51 min. Participants were compensated with a $15 e‐gift card.

### Data Analysis

#### Qualitative Analysis

Semi‐structured interview transcriptions were analyzed using thematic analysis [30] and constant comparison [31]. The mPIs developed an initial deductive code list a priori based on the interview guide, and applied inductive coding methods for codes emergent from the data [32]. The full research team refined the codebook through four analytic retreats to iteratively identify additional inductive codes, which were added and revised until achieving thematic saturation [33]. After finalizing the codebook, five staff independently coded transcripts using NVivo (QSR International) until establishing inter‐rater reliability (Kappa > 0.80) [30]. Staff then coded all transcripts in teams of two, resolving discrepancies through discussion. Research staff reviewed all segments for each code to develop code summaries that synthesized patterns and themes [34].

#### Quantitative Analysis

We performed descriptive statistics to describe participants’ demographic and clinical characteristics using IBM SPSS Statistics (Version 28).

#### Potential for Infection Contraction and Transmission

Participants desired information about the probability, duration, and curability of contracting “infections,” “viruses,” “parasites,” and “diseases” from the pig kidney. Participants expressed concerns about the potential harms of such infections and desired information about which infectious diseases the pig kidney could transmit, and the probability of transmitting those diseases to others. If they were to contract an infectious disease from the pig, participants wanted to know if the transmissible disease was “curable,” and if so, the treatment's side effects, and how long the potential “harm” of the disease and treatment would last. Participants commented: “What potential viruses that can happen… Is there any potential viruses that I can give to my family members or to the public.” (NU#3004) “You know, like there are some infections that are curable and easy to treat. I don't want to have a bigger issue that needs more attention, more bloodwork, more medicine. That's not a good thing.” (LU#3004)

#### Risks, Benefits, and Impact of Xenotransplant Trials

Participants desired information about the trial's overall risks and benefits of participation. Specifically, they sought information about the trial's risks of graft rejection and graft longevity. This included any “unforeseen” “short‐term and long‐term repercussions” or “complications.” Participants wished to be informed about the expected “life span” of the pig kidney, including the likelihood of experiencing kidney rejection or failure due to other causes, as well as how the transplant might impact their life expectancy. As one participant stated: “Well hell, does it work and how long will this last? I'm not trying to do this again. I don't want to be sick again.” (NU#3012)

Moreover, participants desired learning how participating in a trial would affect their “quality of life,” when compared to their quality of life on dialysis. These participants desired assurances that their quality of life would improve as a result of trial participation. These issues were conveyed by one participant: “Did someone live an extended life? Did they not have additional health issues or problems that were related? How were the drugs? How many drugs do they have to take? What's the post‐op treatment like? I mean, I would have to know all those types of details before I would even consider, strongly consider it.” (NU#3013)

#### Xenotransplant Clinical Trial and Recipient/Participant Experience

Participants reported wanting to be informed of “anything and everything” relating to the trials, including “the full breadth of anything that might go wrong.” Specifically, participants desired knowing the number of trials completed, the number of pig kidney transplants performed, and the functional outcomes to date. As one participant questioned: “What generation of trial this is? You know, how far along in the trials we are? How many … pig transplants have been done prior, and how far along are they?” (LU#3008)

Participants also desired information about the experiences of previous pig kidney trial participants, including the side effects and complications of the transplant procedure and post‐transplant medications. Further, participants desired “success stories” that previously enrolled pig transplant recipients would have potentially experienced. After participating in a pig kidney trial, participants would want to remain apprised of the results of the trial, to know how their “role” in the trial had “made a difference” or a “contribution” to the field of xenotransplantation.

#### Clinical Trial Logistics

Participants recognized the importance of post‐transplant monitoring obligations for kidney function and “complications.” Participants specifically wanted to know logistical information regarding the “where,” “schedule,” “frequency” of the “testing and appointments,” and “how long” they would need to receive monitoring. Some also desired details of the medications they would need to take, as well as other expectations, including exercise, and what diet and drinks they could consume. A few participants inquired into “a backup plan” or “alternatives” if the xenotransplant failed and they needed to return to dialysis. Specifically, participants questioned whether they would go to the top or bottom of the allotransplant waitlist, or if they would remain eligible for an allotransplant if the pig kidney failed.

#### The Pig and Its Kidney

#### Health History and Status of the Pig and Its Kidney

Overall, participants wanted assurance that the pig was “a good healthy pig” and its kidney was “functioning,” “healthy,” and “top notch.” One participant stated: “How healthy is it. When a human goes to test to see if they could donate, they run all kinds of tests, yeah? But that's from head to toe of blood work, but for the pig, I'd like to know how healthy the kidney was…how it was filtering prior to its death. I would think that would matter. I'm not a scientist, but I would think it would matter.” (NU#3019)

All participants wanted information about the history and health status of the pig and its kidney prior to participating in a trial. Participants wanted to know what “health concerns” or “life‐threatening diseases” the pig may have had, especially ones that could have impacted its kidney. A few participants wanted to know if the pig had been “genetically altered,” and if so, information related to the genetic modifications. Some desired assurances that the pig and its kidney had been “screened well” to ensure they were free of viruses and diseases, including diabetes and high blood pressure.

#### How the Pig Lived and Died

Participants desired details of how the pig lived and died. They wanted to know about the “environment” in which the pig was raised, including ensuring “there was no abuse” and that the pig was not “raised angry.” Additionally, they were interested in the pig's diet, including if it had been “grass‐fed” and “how much fat” it had been fed, the pig's age and weight, and whether it had been “active.” A few participants also wanted to know non‐clinical, personal information about the pig, such as its name and what it looked like.

Participants wanted to know “the cause of death,” whether it was “euthanized” or died of other causes, and “how long it was dead for” prior to its kidney being procured. Participants were motivated to seek such information to be informed of factors that might impact the health of the pig kidney.

### Informed Consent Form Prototype Feedback

Overall, participants’ first impressions of the informed consent prototype were mixed. Some expressed positive thoughts, describing the prototype as “very thorough,” “easy to read,” and covering “every question that came to the top of [their] head.” Participants also appreciated the “honesty” of the content, noting that the prototype did not “sugar coat” information. As one participant stated: “It isn't a pie‐in‐the‐sky document… it's also telling you about the worst‐case scenario. I think it's a good description of all the different pieces of what can go wrong.” (LU#4101)

By contrast, some participants responded negatively, stating that the prototype was “kind of long,” needed “better detail,” and had sections that “could be better explained in a more positive way.” A few participants voiced their hesitancy to participate in a pig kidney xenotransplant trial based on the information in the prototype. Participants commented: “[My] general impression was that the way it's written here, I probably would not ever volunteer to do the study. I think that there are a lot of negatives and not enough positives…” (LU#4103)

Participants recommended text clarifications and additions to the prototype. For example, adding more details about the pig and pig kidney, including the pig's age and life expectancy and a “comparison of patients transplanted with human kidneys and pig kidneys” as it relates to risk for infection. Participants wanted details about insurance coverage, what would be financially covered by the study, and coverage of non‐FDA‐approved medication. Participants suggested adding details to the monitoring section, including the length of time that patients will be monitored and “what close contacts and relatives [will be] monitored for.” Additionally, participants suggested the prototype include information about “the experience of the surgeon and the surgical team,” to address the question: “Has [the surgeon] done this before or not?”

When asked “How would looking at this consent form make you feel?” most related that they would feel a “bit uneasy,” “a little unsettled,” and that the consent form “would scare me.” Although the consent form made participants uneasy, some clarified that feeling that way seemed appropriate because “you should really think about this before you sign up for it.” One participant further explained that the information “…opened my eyes a bit more. I didn't realize how it could affect so many aspects of my life as opposed to a regular transplant.”

When asked “Has this informed consent template raised new questions that you had not thought of before looking at it?” some related that all their questions had been answered, while others stated that they wanted more information about the research, data on pig kidney transplants, and the transmission of porcine infectious diseases. One participant explained that “There's a lot of things that prompted me to have more questions. For a basic consent I think it's good, but for me I need to have more like science information. But I think it's good, it's uncomfortable but it makes me hopeful.”

Overall, usability testing participants’ preparedness to decide to participate in a pig kidney xenotransplant trial increased in the proportion reporting being “very” or “completely” prepared after having reviewed the informed consent form prototype (prior to review: 12.5%; after review: 31.3%; n.s., p < 0.18) (Table 4).

## Discussion

Our mixed‐methods study of information kidney transplant candidates need to provide informed consent for hypothetical first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trials revealed five domains of information. Kidney transplant candidates desired extensive information about the trial itself, the trial logistics, the impact of the trial on patient health and quality of life, the pig, and the pig's kidney.

We found that patients desired information about the status of the clinical trial as well as the trial logistics. Specifically, trial status characteristics included the number of participants to date and their outcomes. Trial logistics included the duration of the trial, and the exit plan should the pig kidney not work. Other research on kidney, liver, heart, and lung transplant candidates’ information needs for other innovative clinical research corroborates our findings [35].

Our findings about patients’ interest in the donor pig's life, death, and health status at the time of organ procurement are novel and may complement two previous recommendations for a xenotransplant trial informed consent form [23, 36, 37]. Neither of those recommendations for consent form information includes conveying the type of information about the pig and pig kidney that our interview participants expressed knowing about. Taking patients’ concerns seriously about the pig is consistent with calls for addressing the “moral status of nonhuman animals and humankind's legal and moral responsibility towards them” [38]. Kidney patients’ desire to know about the donor pig is similar to some allotransplant recipients’ interest in knowing about the donor of the organ they received [39].

We developed an informed consent prototype that should guide the informed consent educational process for prospective xenotransplant trial participants. Our usability testing interviews found that while the prototype was clear, further details were requested. In the absence of trial specifics, placeholders for those details were added to the prototype. The prototype feedback revealed novel insights into patients' trial concerns. Specifically, some felt “uneasy” or afraid after reviewing the prototype but realized how feeling that way was important for recognizing the broad impact that participation in such a trial could have on their lives.

The informed consent process for first‐in‐human xenotransplant clinical trials should address patients’ information needs to facilitate informed decision‐making. By providing a patient‐centered perspective about information to disclose to prospective xenotransplant trial participants, our findings may guide the development of information guidelines that extend beyond the standard elements of human research informed consent to be disclosed as part of the informed consent process for xenotransplant clinical trials. Moreover, regulatory guidance would be especially valuable to prepare IRBs to review informed consent forms for xenotransplant trials [23].

A systematic review and meta‐analysis of participants’ understanding of informed consent in clinical trials found that half of the participants understood risks and side effects of trials (51.4%) [40]. Subgroup analysis showed that phase I trial participants had a lower understanding of options after withdrawal, understanding of voluntary participation, and ability to name at least one risk than phase II/III participants; critically ill participants had a lower understanding of study purpose, risks, and benefits compared to non‐critically ill participants [40]. Upon initiating first‐in‐human xenotransplant trials, evaluating comprehension of all informed consent components will be critical to determine whether the disclosure process may need revision to enhance patients’ and families’ decision‐making process. Future research should assess patients’ actual decision‐making, information needs, and comprehension upon trial initiation.

In the pig kidney xenotransplant clinical trial context, sufficient time will be needed in the consent process to disclose extensive information, support question asking and discussion, ascertain whether the patient has adequately comprehended disclosed information, and assess the patient's voluntariness about trial participation. A multidisciplinary team approach will be valuable for relating the aforementioned desired types of information to facilitate understanding without information overload. A psychiatric consult will be vital for evaluating patient's comprehension and voluntariness. Ensuring that patients have enough time to reflect on the prospect of trial participation in light of their values and life goals may be accommodated through a 1–2 week cooling off period, commonly used among living donors. However, time may be limited amongst patients whose dialysis access has run out. In such circumstances, the time frame may need to be expedited while also protecting patients’ voluntariness. An independent patient advocate may help protect the patient's voluntary decision making.

Strengths of our study include the multi‐site design, increasing the representativeness and transferability of study findings. Using a mixed‐methods approach generated greater insights than use of a single method. Consultation with our Advisory Committee on the semi‐structured interview guide and informed consent prototype enhanced the accuracy and presentation of our informed consent form prototype thereby increasing the validity of our findings. Our sample size of semi‐structured interviews was appropriate for deriving themes in qualitative research [30] and for usability testing.

This study has limitations. Participants included waitlisted kidney transplant candidates because, while eligibility for a pig kidney xenotransplant trial remains a topic of debate, emerging opinions during data collection suggested candidates would be optimal trial participants [41, 42, 43]. Non‐waitlisted patients could have offered other viewpoints. Participants’ perceptions reflected consideration of hypothetical xenotransplant trial participation, rather than of an actual trial. While participants were waitlisted for 2 years, on average, it is unlikely that their information needs would differ from patients’ waitlisted longer. Waitlist time made no difference in candidates’ information needs about participating in other innovative transplant research [35]. The news of two living humans who received a pig kidney at the time of usability testing may have shaped participants’ desire for information needs. However, this is unlikely as the two recipients did not participate in a clinical trial that could have generated systematic information about outcomes that participants desired.

## Conclusion

Our findings suggest that kidney patients would require extensive information to provide informed consent for participating in a first‐in‐human pig kidney xenotransplant trial. Transplant programs preparing to conduct trials should address these information needs to optimize the informed consent process.
